title: A new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34)
hookLine: a law written on hearts, not stone; the words echo at every Mass

lines: A PROMISE IN A FALLING CITY.
THE BLOOD OF THE NEW COVENANT.
cards: Jerusalem is surrounded. The Temple will burn. And in the middle of all that bad news, a prophet is told to write down a promise.
It holds a phrase Catholics hear over the chalice at every Mass: the blood of the new and eternal covenant. New compared to what? That word didn't start at the Last Supper.
It started with Jeremiah, in a city about to fall. Some scholars call these chapters the Book of Consolation.

teach.h: NOT LIKE THE COVENANT OF STONE.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the days shall come, saith the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Juda."
Not like the old one, made when God took their fathers by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, the one they broke. That covenant was written on stone, two tablets carried down a mountain.
This time the writing moves: "I will give my law in their bowels, and I will write it in their heart."

Bowels sounds odd to us, but in older English it meant the innermost part of a person, the gut, where you feel things before you think them. The law won't be outside you, pressing in. It'll be inside you, pressing out.
No one will need to teach his neighbor, saying know the Lord, because all of them will know me, from the least to the greatest, and I will forgive their sin and remember it no more.
Centuries later, Luke tells us, Jesus took the cup at supper and said, in the Douay: "This is the chalice, the new testament in my blood."
In the Bible, testament and covenant translate the same word: berit in Hebrew, diatheke in Greek, testamentum in Latin. That's where the name New Testament comes from.

teach.h: I WILL WRITE IT IN THEIR HEART.
teach.b: The Letter to the Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's whole passage. Catholics hear it fulfilled in Christ and renewed at every Mass.
Jews read it as God's lasting promise to Israel and Judah, and the Catholic Church teaches that God's covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked.

how: At every Mass the priest speaks over the chalice of the blood of the new and eternal covenant, and Jeremiah 31:31–34 is read in the Church's lectionary, including in Lent.

o: the Ten Commandments carved on two tablets
a peace treaty between Israel and Babylon
God's bond, written on the heart, not on stone

p: old English for the innermost part

s: the phrase new covenant first appears at the Last Supper
it comes from Jeremiah 31, long before. Jesus takes it up over the cup.
testamentum in Latin, diatheke in Greek, berit in Hebrew: the same idea.
the Catholic Church teaches God's covenant with the Jewish people was revoked
the Church teaches it has never been revoked.

games.q: you're Jeremiah. the city is about to fall, and the people have broken the covenant God wrote on stone. what does God promise next?
o: a new set of stone tablets, harder to break.
a law written inside them, on the heart.
no law at all from now on.
games.why: "I will give my law in their bowels, and I will write it in their heart." not a stronger tablet: a different place to write.

practice: Put a hand on your chest if you like, and think of one thing you know is right without anyone telling you: telling a friend the truth, not mocking someone who's down, keeping a promise.
Some readers hear Jeremiah's promise in that kind of writing. If you pray, thank God for what's written there, and ask for what's still blank.

wordCard.voice: New covenant. Jeremiah's promise of a bond with God written on the heart, not on stone; the words Jesus took up over the cup at the Last Supper. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: covenant, a binding promise between two parties. Greek diatheke and Latin testamentum translate it.

carryVoice: Your line: written on the heart. Not on stone this time. Day four hundred twenty-three, done.
